label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
**The Long Version of the Busing Project Text**

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.” Half the group chat agreed with her, or at least piled on with the crying-laughing reacts, which is basically agreement. I’m not mad at her. I get it. She’s known me since we were student teaching at the same school in 2012, and she left teaching in 2019 for HR at a biotech in Cambridge, so she has a very clear memory of what teaching cost and a very clear view from the other side of what jobs can ask of you. She’s not wrong that I could get burned.

But I’d rather explain this once, properly, than argue in fifteen texts. So here’s the long version. It’s for all of you, but it’s really for Jess.

The project is for my juniors, US History II, two sections. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974–76—busing, desegregation, what people remember, what they don’t, what got passed down and what got buried. They record about ten minutes and write a two-page reflection. That’s it. I’ve done it for four years at Cobb Street High and never had a complaint before this one.

The complaint came as an email to my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and it cc’d a school committee member. The parent said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” I have a meeting with Halvorsen and the parent Thursday, Nov. 19, at 3:15.

Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. Quietly is the part I can’t do. I’m not trying to pick a fight with the parent. I actually think she has a point about pressure. That’s the part I’ve been chewing on. I don’t want some kid sitting across from their grandmother feeling like they’ve been assigned to prosecute her. That’s not the assignment. The assignment is to ask questions and listen. There’s a difference between “tell me what you remember” and “tell me why you were wrong.” I think the project mostly gets that right, but I can hear where she’s coming from.

So my plan is to keep it, but add a real alternate. Kids can interview a librarian or archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years with permission, so no kid has to interview family. Nobody is forced to sit down with a grandparent. The skill goal stays the same: ask a real person real questions, listen, put it in context, reflect. If a kid wants the family interview, it’s there. If they don’t, there’s another way through. That seems like the line to me. The kids who are uncomfortable are often the ones who need it most, but I don’t get to force anyone. That’s the line.

I keep thinking about D., a kid in 2023. He interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in ’74. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, not her husband, nobody. D. played forty seconds of the recording for the class and nobody said a word for about a minute. Not a joke, not a cough. Just silence. I’ve been in classrooms for a while now and I don’t get a minute of silence very often.

Then last year a girl found out her uncle threw rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. Not because she wrote something neat or redemptive. Because she was actually thinking. She was trying to hold a family story and a city story at the same time, and she didn’t get to make it simple.

That’s what this project does that the textbook doesn’t. The textbook gives Boston busing one paragraph. One. This is the history of the city they live in. They ride past the streets. Their families are in it, or adjacent to it, or came here after it and inherited the shape of it without the story. I’m not asking them to judge their grandparents. I’m asking them to find out what happened and what it did to people. Those aren’t the same thing.

And yes, I’m scared. A little. I’m not brave about this. I don’t feel like some heroic teacher in a movie. I feel like a guy with a mortgage and a project he believes in and a meeting on Thursday. I’m tenured—since 2021—so I’m not sitting there worried about being fired tomorrow. But tenure isn’t a force field. Halvorsen controls my schedule and who gets AP. I like my job. I want to keep it. I also want to keep doing it in a way I can live with.

Jess, I know you’re not telling me to cave. You’re telling me not to be dumb. Fair. But “one assignment” is doing a lot of work in that text. It’s one assignment the way a wedding is one party. It’s the part of the year where the past stops being a paragraph in a book and becomes a person in a chair. I’m not torching my job. I’m trying to do it. I don’t need you to agree with me. I’d just like you to understand why I’m not going to let it disappear quietly.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. Probably from my car. Probably with too many typos.
